summary: An island nation in the Caroline Islands of the western Pacific, made up of the four states of Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae; it has been in a Compact of Free Association with the United States since 1986.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1885 Spain and Germany contested the Caroline Islands; after arbitration by Pope Leo XIII they went to Spain, and Spanish Capuchin missionaries soon arrived to preach. After Germany bought the islands in 1899 the Catholic Church continued to grow, and during the Japanese rule of 1914–1945 the Japanese authorities even invited Spanish Jesuits to evangelize in the South Seas. As a result Catholicism became the majority faith in Chuuk and Yap states.

ranking.name: Protestantism (United Church of Christ and others)
ranking.description: In 1852 missionaries of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM), a Congregationalist mission society, came from Hawaii to Pohnpei and Kosrae, translated the Bible into the islanders' languages and opened schools. The chiefs and inhabitants of Kosrae converted to Protestantism almost entirely, and to this day Kosrae remains a predominantly Congregational island that strictly observes the Sabbath on Sunday; these churches later formed the United Church of Christ.

ranking.name: Others (Mormon, Seventh-day Adventist, etc.)
ranking.description: After World War II the United States governed Micronesia as a United Nations trusteeship (1947–1986), and American denominations such as the Mormons, Seventh-day Adventists, Assemblies of God and the Baha'i Faith were introduced one after another; they are small but have gradually grown in the towns.

religion.background: The Micronesian islands originally worshipped ancestral spirits and nature deities. In the mid-19th century American Protestant missionaries arrived first in Pohnpei and Kosrae, and during the Spanish and German rule of the late 19th century Catholicism was introduced to Chuuk and Yap. Although the Japanese period brought Shinto and Buddhism, these disappeared with Japan's defeat in 1945. More denominations arrived during the American trusteeship, and Christianity has since become the faith of almost the entire population, with the churches and the traditional chiefly system together forming the pillars of society.

ranking.name: Chuukese
ranking.description: Chuukese belongs to the Micronesian language group and is the language of Chuuk, the most populous state (about half of the national population). Chuuk Lagoon was an important Japanese naval base in World War II, and after the war migration between the states has also given Chuukese a considerable number of speakers in places such as the capital, Pohnpei.

ranking.name: Pohnpeian
ranking.description: Pohnpeian is the language of Pohnpei State, where the capital Palikir is located, and has a complex honorific system used when speaking to the traditional paramount chief, the Nahnmwarki. In the 19th century American missionaries were the first to devise a writing system for it using the Latin alphabet.

ranking.name: Kosraean
ranking.description: Kosraean is spoken only on the single island of Kosrae State; it has few speakers, but almost all the island's inhabitants speak it. In the 19th century missionaries used it to translate the Bible, and the church has played an important role in preserving the language.

ranking.name: Yapese
ranking.description: Yapese is spoken on the main island of Yap and differs considerably from the other Micronesian languages, so its classification is disputed. Yap is known for preserving its traditional culture, for example its giant stone money, while the outer islands of Yap use several other languages.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: From 1947 to 1986 the United States governed the area as a United Nations trusteeship, and English became the language of schools and government. After independence in 1986 and the signing of the Compact of Free Association with the United States, English remained the official language and the common language among the four states, but very few people speak it as a mother tongue.

language.history: The four states of the Federated States of Micronesia each have their own Austronesian language, and the languages are not mutually intelligible. In the 19th century American missionaries devised writing systems for Pohnpeian, Kosraean and others. Spain (1886–1899), Germany (1899–1914) and Japan (1914–1945) then ruled in succession; during the Japanese period Japanese-language education was promoted, leaving many Japanese loanwords. After World War II the American trusteeship made English the language of education and administration, and after independence in 1986 English became the common official language among the states.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: A large, starchy fruit that can be roasted, boiled or fried, or fermented in an earth pit for preservation; its texture is similar to bread or potato.
ranking.history: Breadfruit is a crop that Austronesian seafarers carried aboard their canoes thousands of years ago as they spread across the Pacific, and in Micronesia it is one of the most important staples. On islands such as Pohnpei, people ferment breadfruit in leaf-lined earth pits, where it keeps for months or even years and is used to survive typhoons and famine. The breadfruit harvest season is also an important time for holding traditional feasts and presenting gifts to the chiefs.

ranking.name: Taro
ranking.description: A root crop grown in wetlands or specially dug pit fields; once boiled or roasted it has a creamy texture and can be eaten as is, mashed, or cooked with coconut milk.
ranking.history: Taro is an ancient crop brought by the Austronesian peoples. On infertile coral atolls, islanders dig deep pits, fill them with humus and grow salt-tolerant giant swamp taro, an important survival technique. In Yap the taro patches are managed by women, and holding a taro patch is closely tied to land rights. Taro is also often offered as a gift at weddings, funerals and chiefly ceremonies.

ranking.name: Sakau (kava)
ranking.description: The root of the kava plant, a member of the pepper family, is pounded on a stone, mixed with water, and the liquid is wrung out through hibiscus bark fibre; it has a numbing, relaxing effect.
ranking.history: Sakau is at the heart of traditional ceremonies in Pohnpei; at the feasts offered to the paramount chief, the Nahnmwarki, men pound it with stones, producing a rhythmic sound. The order of drinking follows rank and status, symbolizing the hierarchy of traditional society. Today there are sakau bars all over Pohnpei, and it remains an indispensable drink for socializing, settling disputes and traditional ceremonies.

ranking.name: Coconut crab
ranking.description: The largest land-dwelling arthropod in the world, usually steamed whole or cooked in coconut milk; the meat is sweet, and the fat in the abdomen is especially rich and fragrant.
ranking.history: Coconut crabs live on the coasts and in the woodlands of tropical islands and can break open coconuts with their powerful claws. On islands such as Kosrae and Pohnpei they are a traditional delicacy, often served at festivals and banquets. Because they grow slowly and have long been heavily harvested, their populations have declined, and some islands have set limits on catching them. They represent the islanders' way of eating from local resources, and also face the challenge of conservation.

ranking.name: Sashimi
ranking.description: Fresh tuna and other catch is sliced raw and eaten with soy sauce and wasabi, or with local lime squeezed on and chili added; the flavor is fresh and sweet.
ranking.history: During the Japanese rule of the South Seas Mandate from 1914 to 1945, large numbers of Japanese immigrants came to Micronesia to develop fishing and commerce, and brought with them the custom of eating raw fish with soy sauce. After World War II the Japanese left, but the habit of eating sashimi remained and merged with the islanders' own tradition of eating raw seafood. Today sashimi is almost a must at weddings, church events and holiday feasts, reflecting the deep legacy of Japanese rule.
